# Letting Models Label and People Certify

The 2.11 labeling engine: blind samples, contracts, and what to ask first. It ships with the `potato-skill` skill:

```
/plugin marketplace add davidjurgens/potato-skill
/plugin install potato-skill@potato
```

---

Potato 2.11 adds a labeling engine: models label every item, people label a
blind random sample, and each contract in the config tests the machine labels
against that sample. The machine labels a contract accepts come with a stated
error bound, and the rest go to people. The researcher gets the dataset and a certificate
saying what was tested, on how many human labels.

It is configured in one `labeling_engine` block, and annotators are served its
requests only under `assignment_strategy: engine`. Potato's own guide is
`docs/labeling-engine/` in the checkout, five pages with every key; this page is
what to decide with the researcher and what I saw when I ran it.

## Corpus size

The engine saves human labels when the corpus is much larger than the human
budget. On a small corpus it can sample most of the corpus and accept nothing,
as it did on the 120-item run below.

I ran it on 120 product reviews with Gemma 12B on vLLM as the only source and a
`selective_risk` contract at 10% error and 0.9 confidence. Gemma was wrong on 8
of the 120 (6.7%), under the target, but the corpus was too small to test the
contract and it never passed. The planner opened 107 calibration
requests and 22 resolve requests, and every one of the 120 delivered labels came
from a person.

So ask how many items there are and how many human labels the researcher can
pay for before proposing it. If every item will get a human label anyway, use an
ordinary assignment strategy.

## What to ask the researcher

| Question | Where the answer goes |
|---|---|
| "How often may an accepted machine label be wrong, and how sure do you need to be?" | `error` and `confidence` on a `selective_risk` contract |
| "Do you need every label to be usable, or a rate, such as the share of toxic posts?" | `selective_risk` for labels; `ppi` for a prevalence with an interval |
| "Should the model match your annotators rather than a fixed accuracy?" | `no_worse_than_human`, which needs `humans.overlap_k` of at least 3 |
| "How many human labels can you pay for?" | `budgets.human_labels` |
| "Which questions should the model answer?" | `labeling_engine.schemas`; free-text questions cannot be among them |

The error target and the confidence are the researcher's call. They are what
the certificate will claim, so do not pick them yourself.

## A minimal block

```yaml
assignment_strategy: engine
annotation_schemes:
  - annotation_type: radio
    name: sentiment
    description: "Overall sentiment?"
    labels: [positive, negative, neutral]
labeling_engine:
  enabled: true
  sources:
    - id: gemma
      kind: llm
      endpoint_type: vllm
      model: google/gemma-4-12B-it-qat-w4a16-ct
      base_url: http://localhost:8001/v1
      confidence: {method: logprob}
  contracts:
    - {id: accuracy, kind: selective_risk, schema: sentiment, error: 0.1, confidence: 0.9}
    - {id: prevalence, kind: ppi, schema: sentiment, confidence: 0.9}
  budgets: {human_labels: 200}
```

`logprob` confidence reads the probabilities of the model's one-letter answer.
It needs a backend that returns logprobs, such as vLLM, and a scheme with at
most 20 labels. `native` on an `llm` source is refused:
`confidence.method native comes from decision models and detectors; an llm
source uses verbalized, k_sample or logprob`.

Contract keys are checked. A misspelt `error` names the key and the ones the
kind reads:
`labeling_engine.contracts[0] (selective_risk) has unknown keys: eror (known:
confidence, error, id, kind, per_class, schema, tolerance)`.

## Free-text questions

The engine labels only schemes it can score a machine answer on, and free text
is not one of them. A contract on a free-text scheme is a validation error:
`these contracts are on schemes the engine cannot score machine answers for:
accuracy (note: text)`.

A free-text scheme can still sit beside the engine's schemes, but under
`assignment_strategy: engine` people see it only on the items the engine sends
them, and `potato validate` says so:

```
assignment_strategy: engine serves only the engine's requests, and the engine
does not label note, so people will answer them only on the items the engine
sends them for the other schemes, not on every item. If every item needs them,
use another assignment_strategy.
```

That is a warning, so `--strict` fails on it. If the researcher needs a comment
on every item, the study cannot use `assignment_strategy: engine`. Tell them
before building it.

## An engine with no contracts

A machine label is accepted only when a contract has tested it. An engine with
`contracts: []` accepts nothing. I enabled one with a `static` source holding
the right answer for all 120 items. It validated clean under `--strict`, opened
62 calibration requests, and accepted no machine label.

## The budget check

`potato validate` works out whether `budgets.human_labels` could certify each
`selective_risk` contract at all:

```
budgets.human_labels 20 cannot certify accuracy (error 0.1, confidence 0.9)
even with no machine errors: it needs at least 54 human labels (27 held out,
the rest for choosing the threshold). Raise the budget or loosen the target.
```

That is the floor for a model that is never wrong. In the 120-item run, 124
answered requests were not enough for a model wrong on 6.7% of the items.

`assignment_strategy: engine` with `labeling_engine.enabled: false` fails
validation: `assignment_strategy: engine serves the labeling engine's requests,
but labeling_engine.enabled is false.`

## Running it

```bash
potato label run config.yaml        # label every item, draw the blind sample
potato start config.yaml -p 8000    # people answer the sample
potato label status config.yaml     # contracts, requests, what is still missing
```

`label run` made 120 model calls on 120 items, opened 62 calibration requests
and accepted nothing: with no human labels yet, the contract read
`insufficient`.

Only one process drives a study. While the server runs, its planner holds the
study's lock, and the command line refuses with exit 2:

```
server:<host>:<pid>:1 is driving this study. Certify through it instead
(POST /api/engine/v1/certify, or the admin page's Certify button), or stop it
first.
```

`status`, `certificate`, `export` and `calls` are read-only and work while the
server runs. The planner certifies on its own as labels arrive, so a running
study rarely needs an explicit certify. `POST /api/engine/v1/certify` with the
admin key in `X-API-Key` worked, and the same route without the key returned
403. The admin page is `/admin/labeling-engine`.

## What annotators see

Every calibration item showed "Label this one yourself. Suggestions are off for
this item." above the form. Calibration requests are blind: the person does not
see a machine answer, so their label is an independent check of it.

## Reading the result

`potato label certificate config.yaml --format md` writes the certificate. A
contract that has not passed says so in its statement:

```
Target, not established: at most 10.0% of accepted labels wrong, with
probability at least 0.90 (overall). No machine label on this scheme is
accepted until it is met (43 held-out labels, look 1).
```

When reporting to the researcher, quote the statement rather than the config:
the config holds the target, and only a `met` statement reports a result.

## Getting the labels out

`potato label export config.yaml --out DIR`, or the `labeling_engine` export
format, writes `labels.jsonl`, `labels.csv`, the certificate as JSON, Markdown
and HTML, a dataset card in `README.md`, and `model_calls.jsonl`. `labels.csv`
has one row per item and scheme:

```
id,schema,label,label_origin,status,source,model,source_version,confidence,contract_version,request_ids
r0001,sentiment,neutral,human,accepted,,,,,,[9]
```

The ordinary `csv` export still holds the annotators' answers. With the engine
on it adds `engine_purpose` and `engine_request` columns, and the second one
holds the request's `split`, `visibility` and `inclusion_prob`. Use them to tell
the blind random sample from the other answers before anyone computes an
accuracy from the human labels.

## Configs with the older keys

`icl_labeling` and `judge_calibration` still work, and each prints a note
pointing at the engine. From 2.11 through 2.13.0, `pre_annotation` printed one
too:

```
NOTE: pre_annotation still works, but the labeling engine now does this: use
labeling_engine (a static source). `potato label migrate-config` writes the
equivalent block. pre_annotation is planned for removal in 3.0.
```

On 2.13.1 it prints nothing, because `pre_annotation` is no longer deprecated.
It shows a model's or an import's answer as an editable starting point. The
engine's `static` source does something else: it accepts a label only where a
contract certifies it. The importers write `pre_annotation` for that reason,
so keep it when the answers are meant to be corrected by hand.

`potato label migrate-config config.yaml --out new.yaml` writes a copy with a
`labeling_engine` block. For `pre_annotation` it wrote a `static` source on the
same field, `enabled: false`, and `contracts: []`. Enabling that block as it
stands accepts nothing (see **An engine with no contracts**), so add the
contract with the researcher before turning it on.

## What I have and have not verified

Run on 2.11.0 (`eb284819`), from a checkout, against Gemma 12B on a vLLM server:

- the 120-item study end to end: `label run`, the server's planner, three
  annotators labeling over HTTP from the items' true labels, `status`,
  `certificate`, `export`, and the `labeling_engine` and `csv` exports;
- the writer-lock refusals of `label certify` and `label run`, `POST
  /api/engine/v1/certify` with and without the admin key, and the admin page;
- every validation message quoted above, by `potato validate --strict` on a
  config built to trigger it;
- `migrate-config` on a `pre_annotation` config, and that block enabled.

Not verified here: decision-model sources (Laya, hosted Jev, OpenJev), the
detector, judge, jury and distilled sources, the `no_worse_than_human`,
`budget_first` and `distributional` contracts, verify requests, crowd
recruiting on Prolific, Pocket Mode with the engine, and the Python SDK.
